title: White Sox Target Top Starting Pitcher in Bold Trade Rumor Push【2024】
body:
The Chicago White Sox announced they will aggressively pursue upgrades to their starting rotation this offseason, acknowledging that the talent that carried the club to a respectable 2026 campaign is not enough to push the team into serious postseason contention in 2027. General manager Chris Getz, speaking with reporters after the club’s elimination by the Cleveland Guardians in the American League Wild Card series, laid out a clear roadmap: add at least one frontline starter and deepen the middle‑of‑the‑rotation pool, while maintaining financial flexibility to retain key pieces on the roster.

Chicago’s 2026 season was a mixed bag. The team finished with a winning record and secured a Wild Card berth, largely on the back of a potent offense that ranked among the league’s top five in runs scored and a bullpen that posted a sub‑3.00 ERA in the final two months. However, the starting staff posted a collective 4.68 ERA, the third‑worst among teams that qualified for the playoffs. The rotation’s inconsistencies were starkly exposed in the postseason, where the White Sox surrendered 12 runs in 14 innings against Cleveland, including a 6‑run outing from rookie left‑hander Garrett Crochet that ultimately sealed the series. Getz noted that while the club’s core—center‑fielder Andrew Benintendi, shortstop Luis Robert and ace right‑hander Dylan Cease—remains intact, the gap between the top of the staff and the back end is too wide to ignore.

The front office’s approach appears to be a blend of targeted free‑agent signings, strategic trades, and internal development. Getz confirmed that the team is monitoring several high‑profile free agents, including veteran right‑hander Kevin Gausman and left‑hander Chris Sale, both of whom could be acquired if the White Sox are willing to dip into the luxury tax threshold. “We are not chasing every name that comes out of the market,” Getz said. “We are looking for a pitcher who can slot into the rotation, command a mid‑to‑high‑90s fastball, and give us depth on the back end without compromising our long‑term flexibility.” The organization is also expected to explore trade possibilities, particularly with teams looking to unload high‑salary arms for prospects. The White Sox have a surplus of catching depth and a promising outfield prospect in Luis Rodriguez, assets that could be leveraged to acquire a mid‑rotation starter.

Internally, Chicago’s farm system continues to produce promising arms that could fill the rotation void. Left‑hander Nick Nastrini, a 2023 first‑round pick, posted a 3.21 ERA across Double‑A and Triple‑A in 2025 and is projected to be MLB‑ready by mid‑2027. Right‑hander Jared Jones, who debuted in September 2025, showed flashes of brilliance with a 2.89 ERA in limited action. Getz emphasized that the club will give these prospects a chance to compete for roster spots, but he also warned that “the margin for error in a playoff‑caliber rotation is razor‑thin.” The front office will likely blend home‑grown talent with external acquisitions to ensure a balanced staff capable of delivering quality starts throughout the grueling 162‑game schedule.

Financially, the White Sox are positioned to make a splash. The team avoided a luxury‑tax penalty in 2026 and retains roughly $45 million in payroll flexibility for the upcoming year, according to MLB financial filings. This cushion enables Chicago to pursue a top‑tier starter without jeopardizing the contract extensions already in place for key hitters and relievers. However, Getz cautioned that the organization is mindful of the long‑term ramifications of overpaying for a single pitcher. “We want to avoid a scenario where we’re stuck with a big contract that limits our ability to improve other areas,” he said. The front office is reportedly consulting with analytics staff to evaluate the cost‑per‑run value of potential acquisitions, ensuring that any investment aligns with the team’s broader competitive window.

The White Sox’s pursuit of rotation upgrades signals a shift from a “good enough” mindset to an ambition of becoming a perennial contender in the American League Central. While the offensive firepower and bullpen stability provide a solid foundation, the front office’s acknowledgment that starting pitching is the missing piece reflects a mature, data‑driven strategy. As free agency looms and trade talks heat up, Chicago fans can expect a flurry of activity in the coming weeks, with the ultimate goal of fielding a staff that can consistently pitch deep into games and give the offense a chance to win.
